idea-plugin.name: Flowable Atlas
idea-plugin.description:
The complete Flowable companion for IntelliJ IDEA. Flowable Atlas turns the model keys and expressions scattered across your Java code and Flowable models into first-class, IDE-aware references — completed, validated and navigable — and maps your whole project into a single interactive explorer. Everything is resolved against the models that actually live in your repository, so a wrong key or a broken expression is caught in the editor, long before deployment.

Zero configuration: open a project that contains the Flowable models you exported from Design (the app .zip / deployment .bar, holding .bpmn / .cmmn / .dmn / .form / .data / .service / …) and start typing. The plugin indexes every model and puts that knowledge to work across four areas. A Flowable Design *-models workspace checked in as loose JSON is one checkbox away, in Settings → Tools → Flowable Atlas.

1 · Model-key intelligence

  • Context-aware key completion at every Flowable API position that takes a model key — process, case, decision, form, event, channel, data object, master data, service, action, agent, knowledge base, template, security policy, query, variable extractor, sequence, SLA, dashboard component, data dictionary, page and unified work definitions. Both org.flowable.* and com.flowable.*. Search by key, by name, or by any fragment — type 0061 to get DEMO-DO-0061.
  • Cascade completion for fluent chains — operation("…") completes the operations of the data object / service resolved from the sibling definitionKey(…) / serviceKey(…) (constant references are resolved), and value("…", …) completes that operation's input fields. DMN variable("…", …) offers the decision's input/output variables.
  • More than keys — completion for message & signal names, process variables, task-definition keys and activity IDs, scoped to the processDefinitionKey / caseDefinitionKey in the same query chain when present, so you see only that model's ids. Ctrl/Cmd-click lands on the <signal> or <userTask> that declares one, and a message or signal no model declares is flagged — an unknown message throws at run time, an unknown signal reaches nobody.
  • Model → model references in BPMN/CMMN XML — the keys that live inside the models themselves (callActivity calledElement, flowable:formKey, decisionRef, CMMN caseRef / processRef) get the same completion, Ctrl/Cmd-click navigation and broken-key inspection as Java call sites — so a calledElement pointing at a missing process is caught before deployment.
  • Broken-key inspection — an unknown key (in Java, in model XML, or inside a JSON model: a form's subform, a data object's backing service, an app's models) is flagged inline with a "did you mean …?" quick-fix to the closest real key.
  • Navigation & Find Usages — Ctrl/Cmd-click a key literal to jump straight to the model file; hover for its type, name and location. Find Usages on a delegate class or an ${bean.method()} expression lists the model files that reference it.
  • Gutter icons, both ways — on a class or method a model uses, a bot class, a REST handler a model calls, each listing those models; beside a model key, the model with its diagram.
  • Go to Model… and Find in Models… — one search over every model key, the elements inside the models and their full text, paths inside .bar / .zip archives included; also the Flowable Model tab of Search Everywhere.
  • Code generation — generate a typed Java constants class (FlowableModelKeys.Process.ORDER_FULFILMENT, model name in Javadoc) that stays in sync as models are added, renamed or removed; typed Java DTOs from one data object (Alt/Option-Enter on its definitionKey("…")) or from whole apps; and Liquibase changelogs from a data object or from the apps, with the plan shown before anything is written.
  • Liquibase aware — inside a changelog it completes <column> names and tableName from the backing service model, and flags columns that no backing Flowable model defines.

2 · Flowable expression language support

  • Both dialects, first-class — the backend JUEL dialect (${…} / #{…}) and the frontend form dialect ({{…}}) each get syntax highlighting, rainbow parentheses and brace matching.
  • Live validation — structural syntax errors, and unknown functions, namespaces or flw.* members, are flagged against a catalog of the real, verified Flowable function set.
  • Expression completion — functions, engine root objects, and your project's own process/case variables and form fields.
  • Recognised inline, everywhere expressions live — BPMN/CMMN/DMN XML, .form / .page JSON, and (optionally) Java string literals — so the highlighting, validation and completion follow you into the models you edit.
  • Real Groovy & JavaScript in script bodies — BPMN/CMMN script tasks, listener scripts and action-bot scripts get the IDE's own language support injected inline: compiler-grade syntax errors, highlighting and fragment editing (Alt-Enter). Groovy is bundled in every IDEA; JavaScript lights up on Ultimate. JUEL or unknown script formats keep the plain expression injection. Atlas additionally runs its own dependency-free structural script check (unterminated strings/comments, unbalanced brackets, scriptFormat typos) in the CLI and the explorer's Checks page.
  • Flowable environments — define your DEV/QA/UAT/PROD servers once for the whole IDE instead of once per repository, and pick them from a list. Each environment holds any of a Flowable Design connection, a Flowable Work connection and the Flowable Control and Hub addresses, which Atlas only opens in a browser (Tools → Flowable Atlas → Open Environment in Browser); the Design pull and the Atlas Playground point independently, so running against QA while models still come from DEV1 is an ordinary way to work. Mark an environment Protected and Atlas asks before pulling from it or evaluating against it. Passwords and tokens stay in the IDE password safe.
  • Atlas Playground (a tool window) — type an expression, pick backend or frontend, and get instant validation and completion; scope completion to one model; evaluate a frontend expression live against a pasted JSON payload; or evaluate a backend expression against a running app through the Flowable Inspect REST API. Which app it runs against is one of your environments, and the fastest way to switch is to paste a Work URL: the environment, the scope and the instance id all fill in from the link.
  • Script Playground (the Scripts tab of the same tool window) — paste or write a Groovy/JavaScript/Python script: the IDE's real language editing (completion, coloring) where the language plugin is available, live structural validation with squiggles and clickable problem rows (the same checks the CLI and the explorer's Checks page runs), the scope variables the script touches as chips, a picker that loads any script task / listener / action-bot script straight from the project's models, and a library of worked examples — a complete, commented script for every context and language, to start from rather than from an empty editor.

3 · Atlas explorer & hub

  • Atlas Hub — a tool window (right stripe) that is the plugin's control center: which Flowable project Atlas is about, how many models it knows and how fresh that is, a health row with the last analysis's defects and advice, one attention line when something needs a hand, and four blocks — the generated explorer, the models opened last, the Flowable Design pull, the playground's runtime — each with its actions beside its state, kept up to date live.
  • Atlas Findings — a tool window (bottom stripe) listing every defect of the project from the same in-process analysis as the explorer, by check, advice on request, each with why it matters and what to do; double-click opens the finding at its line, and Accept… records a reason in the output folder's waivers.json, the file the explorer and the CLI's gate read. Swing, so it works under Remote Development.
  • Map your whole project — Tools → Flowable Atlas → Generate → Atlas Explorer… turns your models + Java + Liquibase into a single self-contained, offline, interactive HTML page. Save it into the project and open it in your browser or right inside the IDE (embedded viewer), then click through every relationship in both directions. In Settings → Tools → Flowable Atlas → Generation you pick exactly which artifacts are written — summary & overview Markdown, the graph JSON, the explorer HTML, a CLAUDE.md primer for AI agents, and a Playwright guide that lets an agent drive Flowable Work in a browser, with this project's stage bars, tasks, required fields and button conditions. Generation runs entirely in-process — no external tools required — and honours the project's expression allowlist.
  • An ER diagram designer — tick ER diagram designer (HTML) under Settings → Tools → Flowable Atlas → Generation and Atlas writes a page of its own beside the explorer: drag the project's tables onto a canvas, show their columns and types, search across every table and column, draw named 1:1 / 1:n / n:m relations, colour them and let Atlas arrange them — for explaining a data model to the business — with SVG/PNG export and a diagram file you can commit; Tools → Flowable Atlas opens it in an editor tab in the IDE's theme. It carries only the tables, so it stays small however large the project is.
  • IDE-native viewing — the embedded explorer follows the IDE light/dark theme (switching restyles live) and carries a toolbar with Regenerate Atlas Explorer, Reload, Open Atlas Playground and Open in Browser.
  • Reopen without regenerating — Open Atlas Explorer (Atlas Hub, or Tools → Flowable Atlas) opens an already-generated *.explorer.html — including one written by the standalone atlas CLI into the configured output folder — as a center editor tab (like a DB table), so you never have to leave the IDE for a browser.

4 · Models in the IDE

  • Text and picture side by side — a process, case, decision, form or page opens with its diagram, decision table or form wireframe beside the text; click an element in the picture to land on its declaration.
  • App archives, opened — a .bar or .zip expands in the Project view, and every model inside it is indexed, navigable and searchable without unpacking.
  • Compare Model with Archive — a model generated into the project folder against its entry in the app export, side by side in the IDE's diff viewer, both laid out first so a minified export still compares line by line.

How it feels

  • runtimeService.startProcessInstanceByKey("<caret>") → your process keys.
  • cmmnRuntimeService.createCaseInstanceBuilder().caseDefinitionKey("<caret>") → your case keys.
  • dataObjectRuntimeService.createDataObjectInstanceQuery().definitionKey(KEY).operation("<caret>") → that data object's operations; .value("<caret>", …) → the operation's fields.
  • Press completion twice to list all model keys of every type, regardless of the call site.

Completion fires inside string literals and at bare arguments alike (inserting a quoted key), with Flowable keys ranked to the top — no setup beyond opening a project that contains your Flowable models.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
0.32.0

  • Storylines: each process and case told in the order a person would. The explorer has a new page, #/flow, that nests what a model's own page lists: a gateway holds its branches, each under its condition and up to the point where they meet; a loop is one step naming the step it goes back to; a boundary event follows the step it is attached to, with its own path and where that rejoins; a call activity, and a process task in a case, is opened one level deep. A case is told by its stages and plan items, each with what it waits for. --flow writes the same stories as flow.json, for a script or for an agent asked to retell a process in prose, which then has the order and the branching in hand instead of reconstructing them from sequence flows. It is not part of --all: the explorer that run writes carries the stories.
  • The IDE's CLAUDE.md names only the artifacts written with it. With Graph (JSON) unticked — on a large project it is the one artifact too big to commit — the file still sent an agent to query graph.json and told the user to tick it. It now leaves the graph's recipes out and sends the agent to the overview for who uses a model.
  • The generated CLAUDE.md says how to read a model inside an archive. Most models of a solution project are entries of an app archive, which the overview names as <archive>.zip!<entry>; the step that says to read the source now gives the command, unzip -p <archive>.zip <entry>.

0.31.2

  • A table grown over many changelog files is listed once. Every changelog carried every column of every table it touches, as the table stands once its run is over. An application that grows a table by one changelog file per release therefore listed a table of four hundred columns eighty times: the Liquibase part of graph.json and of the explorer's page grew with files × columns, and on a real project it was 121 MB of a 172 MB graph.json. A table that several changelogs of one run shape is now listed under one of them — the one a service reads the table from, else the one that created it — and the others name that changelog in columnsIn; in the explorer their pages link there. Which file added a column is still on the column, and what a file did is in its change sets. A project whose tables are each built by one changelog is unchanged. A --changes run against a graph.json written by an earlier version lists the changelogs that now point elsewhere as changed once.

0.31.1

  • graph.json is smaller, and a nested form no longer grows with its depth. A key whose value would be null is not written: .file and .resultVariable answer null either way, so a jq query that tests a value reads the same, and one that tests has(...) should test the value instead. A form field names only the nearest container that can hide, disable or ignore it, as containerGate, and that container names the next one out; containerGates, the list of every container around a field, is gone. And a model that sits in the project twice, in an app archive and beside it, no longer gives its variables each parameter mapping and script site twice. Together that is 3 to 6 % on the projects it was measured on and a third on a form nested ten panels deep. A --changes run against a graph.json written by 0.31.0 lists the forms with gated fields as changed once, until the baseline is regenerated.
  • A case's plan tree says what each plan item waits for, by name. A criterion read entry on planItemprocessTask14: a plan item's id, which no line of the tree carries, without the transition the sentry waits for. It now reads entry on complete "Assessment" if …. A name that repeats in the case is said with its stage, or with its id where a sibling carries the same one. The line says how its parts combine: the on-parts of one sentry are joined by and, a second criterion of the same kind starts with or. A sentry with neither an event nor a condition reads at once where it printed a bare entry, (triggerMode=onEvent) marks a sentry whose event and condition have to coincide, and an exit that completes its stage says so (exitEventType=forceComplete). In the overview and in --slice.
  • A task says what it hands over and what it assigns. A process or case task in a case carries its in and out mappings, as a call activity does: in(orderId→reviewedOrder) in("express"→priority) out(total→total). A quoted source is a literal, a bare one a variable, an expression is a code span, and a mapping without a source keeps its arrow where it printed None→target. A task that initializes variables lists its assignments, in a case and in a process: set(approved=false) set(stage="Intake"). Its line used to end at the delegate expression every such task shares.
  • A variable's slice says who sets it, who reads it and what a mapping assigns. Used by listed a model that only ever sets the variable beside the ones that read it; each model now carries sets, reads or sets and reads. Set by and Read by show the other end of a mapping: the value an assignment sets, the variable of the called model an out-parameter copies, the variable a read is copied to.
  • A form's slice lists every field, and a shared data source is listed once. The overview stops at 40 fields and points at the graph; a slice is the page of that one form and sent its reader there for the last few. Nine selects on one URL were nine identical lines and are one, with ×9.
  • The generated CLAUDE.md offers the slice for every kind of node. It showed --slice process:<key> alone, so an agent given a form, a case or a Java class had to guess that the slice takes it, and one asked about a variable read the graph instead. The step names case:, form:, variable: and java: ids, and says how to take one step, plan item or field out of a large slice: its line is complete in itself, so | grep -i '<its name>' is the answer. The graph step says where a model body of another type lives and that a body can run to tens of kilobytes.
  • A literal in a form binding is no variable. {{true}}, {{false}} and {{null}} — what a script button assigns, what a hidden field is set to — gave a project three variables of those names, each used by every form that binds the literal. A word of JavaScript ({{Math.max(a, b)}}), a call ({{round(total)}}) and the namespace of one of the project's own frontend functions are no variables either.

0.31.0

  • A gateway flow that can never be taken is a finding. The new defect shadowedFlow reports the default, and every flow listed after it, when an exclusive gateway has a flow without a condition ahead of them: the engine takes the first flow whose condition holds, and a flow without one always holds. An unconditional flow written last works as an implicit default and is not reported. The sample project shows one, and Atlas now runs twenty-six checks.
  • --baseline gates what a change adds, not the backlog. Most real projects fail --fail-on defects on their first run. With --baseline <path>, --fail-on matches only findings the baseline does not have. The path can be a graph.json from an earlier run, or the target branch's checkout or archive, which is analysed in the same run. An archive is read under any name: git show "$BASE:apps/app.zip" > base.zip is the quick way to get the base of a pull request, and a file that fails to parse in both versions is not called new. Findings are compared by check, model, element and subject, so a reworded message does not count as new. Every report still lists every finding, and the verdict says how many it left to the baseline.
  • What a change did to the models, for reviewing a pull request. Git shows a commit to an app archive as a binary change, so a reviewer sees nothing of what it does to a process. --changes --baseline <base> writes APP_OVERVIEW.changes.md, or prints it with --stdout, and --all with --baseline writes <project>.changes.md beside the other artifacts. The report lists every model added, removed or changed, with the tasks, flows, form fields and rules that came, went or changed in each. It also lists the references added and removed, and the findings the change brought and the ones it resolved. It is short enough for a pull-request comment or a CI step summary. A model kept in two files, such as a Design export beside its -bar.zip, counts as changed when either copy changes, and the report names the file when only the copy Atlas does not show changed (graph.json lists such models under modelCopies).
  • A red --fail-on run names the findings that made it red. The log used to show only counts per check. After the count line it now lists the matching findings, worst first and one per line: severity, check, file and line (or node id), model and element, and message. It lists the first 50, then says where to read all of them.
  • --annotate github puts those findings on the pull request. The same findings are printed as GitHub Actions workflow commands on stdout, which GitHub shows as annotations on the run and on the pull request's files. Paths are relative to the working directory, so run the job from the checkout's root. A model inside an archive gets no line number, because GitHub can only point at the archive.
  • --junit <file> writes the findings as a JUnit report for CI test views. GitLab's merge-request widget, Jenkins, Azure DevOps and GitHub test reporters show one suite per check and one testcase per finding. A finding keeps the same name from run to run. A finding the gate matches is a failure that says why it matters and what to do. Waived, ungated and baselined findings are skipped, each with its reason.
  • A CLAUDE.md the CLI writes tells an agent how to check its model edit. Its start-here procedure now ends with the command that reruns Atlas with --baseline against the generated graph.json and --fail-on defects. An agent sees each defect its change added before it reports done.
  • A waiver file that waives less than it seems to now says why. A syntax error is reported with the file's name, line and column, not as "waivers.json is not a JSON object". A rule naming a check Atlas does not know is reported with the nearest check id, and the rule is kept. A top-level key nothing reads is reported, because the explorer's Save would drop it. Above all this is rules, which is what graph.json calls them. A waivers or notes that is not a list is reported too. A --waivers path that does not exist is now said on stderr; before, it waived nothing without a word.
  • A finding opens on the line it is about. Each finding now carries the line of its element's declaration, of the reference that names a missing model, of the expression, or of the script line a script problem is on. A script problem used to give its line within the script as a line of the model. The explorer's open button, the IDE's Findings panel and the overview's file:line now land on that line, inside archives too.
  • A missing model says who references it. A missingRefs finding names the model that references the missing key, and how many more do, and opens on that reference. It used to name only the missing key.
  • An expression finding names the models that hold the expression. The summary, CLAUDE.md and the overview say which models contain an invalid or suspect expression. The finding opens there when a single model holds it, and a model's --slice now lists the problems of its expressions.
  • A task whose every outgoing flow is conditional needs a default too. gatewayNoDefault now also reports a task, event or subprocess that leaves only through conditional flows and has no default flow. When none of the conditions holds, the engine throws "no outgoing sequence flow" there, just as it does at a gateway. The count line now reads choices with no way out.
  • Two flows that are exact opposites always leave a way out. ${x}/${!x}, ${a == b}/${a != b} and vars:isEmpty/vars:isNotEmpty are no longer reported by gatewayNoDefault. == true/== false still are, because both are false when the value is unset.
  • An error boundary counts only when it can catch the failure. Only a BPMN error reaches an error boundary event or an error event subprocess. A mail or HTTP task behind one is therefore reported by unguardedTasks unless it maps its failure with flowable:mapException, and the messages and the suggested fix now say so.
  • An HTTP task with handleStatusCodes is no longer treated as handled. The engine turns those status codes into the BPMN error HTTP<code>, which fails the instance when nothing catches it. The task is now reported until an error boundary or an error event subprocess is there to catch it, even when ignoreException is set.
  • A task that only ever runs inside a timer's or an async step's job is no longer told its exceptions reach a caller. unguardedTasks now treats a synchronous task like an async one when every path to it starts at a timer or an async step with no wait state in between.
  • A vars: call with the wrong number of arguments is an invalid expression. ${vars:get('route', 'A')} makes the engine read 'route' as the variable container and fail at runtime, and ${vars:equals(x)} is an argument short. Both are now invalidExpr errors in the reports, and the IDE's expression inspection flags them too. ${vars:get(execution, 'x')} stays valid.
  • Models the platform ships are no longer reported as missing. A reference to one of the platform's default forms, permission decisions, templates, documents, actions or security policies now resolves to a platform-provided model. That includes the F07-deactivateUser form that a copied deactivate-user.action keeps, which used to be a missingRefs error and failed --fail-on error. A misspelt key, or the same key used for another kind of model, is still reported, and the IDE's broken-key inspections draw the same line.
  • A repository without service models no longer reports its changelogs as orphans. When a project defines no service and no data object, its models are deployed from elsewhere. A changelog that names a service the project lacks is then no longer a changelogIssues finding.
  • A script may use task or execution as its own variable names. Closure, loop, catch, function and arrow parameters now shadow the engine's bindings the same way a declaration does. So tasks.any { task -> … } in a script task is no longer reported as using a task that the context does not bind.
  • Calls to the methods of the engine's own objects are no longer typos. A script may call any method of the entity the engine binds, such as execution.getRootProcessInstance() or caseInstance.setName(…), and scriptIssues no longer suggests the nearest documented method instead. Completion still offers only the documented interface.
  • A script service operation's body is checked. The script of a script-type service operation (config.script) runs only when something calls the operation, and Atlas did not look at it, so a body that could never run was found by its first caller. It is now validated in its own context — the flw API and the operation's inputs, by name, and no execution — reported as scriptIssues on the operation, shown on the operation's card on the service's page, where the finding opens it, and listed on the explorer's Scripts page under Service scripts. The Script Playground offers the context too, with an example.
  • A TODO in a BPMN, CMMN or DMN file names the element it sits in. The finding jumps to that element, and a sentry is shown by the diamond of its criterion. A TODO with nothing after it is identified by that element and what carries it (sentry2/documentation) instead of by its line, so accepting it survives an edit above it.
  • A broken palette, dashboard component, user definition or tenant setup is a parse issue. A truncated .palette or .dashboardcomponent came out as a record with no key that nothing could show. An unparseable .user.json, tenant setup or master-data rows file was dropped, and so was one above the 32 MB limit. None of this was reported, although the platform fails to deploy or start on a broken one. Each is now reported like any other model that does not parse: a parse diagnostic and a parseIssues error naming the file. An oversized one is a skip warning, like an oversized model.
  • A malformed XML file is reported with its line, and -q stays quiet. A BPMN, CMMN or DMN model or a Liquibase changelog that was not well-formed made the XML parser print its own [Fatal Error] :2:3: … to stderr, even under -q, and the parse issue named the file but not the line. Nothing is printed now. The parseIssues finding carries the line, so the explorer and the IDE open the file there, and -v prints path:line.
  • Alt+Enter opens the explorer page of a Java class, method or REST handler. On the name of a class or method a model uses, or of a REST handler, Open in Atlas Explorer opens its class, method or endpoint page: roles and bean names, the models using it, an endpoint's callers and parameters. The gutter marks only list the models.
  • A broken model key inside a JSON model is flagged in the editor. A form component's subform, a data object's backing service, an app's models or a channel's event that names no model used to deploy without a word, although the report calls it a missing reference. The new inspection Unknown Flowable model key (model JSON) flags it, with a fix to the nearest key.
  • Messages, signals and task keys in Java are links, and an unknown one is flagged. Ctrl+click on signalEventReceived("…"), startProcessInstanceByMessage("…"), taskDefinitionKey("…") or activityId("…") lands on the <signal>, <message> or <userTask> that declares it, and Ctrl-Q names the model. The new inspection Unknown Flowable message, signal or task name flags a message or signal that no model declares: an unknown message throws at run time, and an unknown signal reaches nobody. It flags a task key or activity id only when the chain names its process. A bare signalRef, or a signal a case's event listener waits for, counts as a name the engine uses. A name a model computes at run time gets no verdict.
  • Event keys the platform ships are no longer flagged in model XML. _flowableMailEvent and its siblings are not missing models, as the report already says. A form key that names a page, or a data-object key that names master data, also counts, as it does at run time.
  • Atlas Findings opens every finding where it is. A double-click or Enter did nothing for a finding with no file of its own, and opened most of the rest at the top of the file. A finding now opens at its line. Without a line (in a minified form, or for a column or a config path) it opens at its element or at what it names. A variable, a service operation or an expression that several models hold opens in the model it lives in, and the window asks which one when there are several. The detail pane's Where: row names that model and how many more there are.
  • Accepting a finding in Atlas Findings updates the explorer too. Accept now regenerates the explorer pages in the folder of the waivers.json it wrote, and an open page reloads where you were reading. The window, the Hub and the page then show the same counts. Before, the page still counted the accepted finding as open. While the pages are regenerated, the window says it is analyzing.
  • An accepted finding stays accepted when the explorer was generated outside the output folder. Accept writes waivers.json next to that page, but the next analysis read the one in the configured output folder, so the finding came back as open. The analysis now reads the file Accept wrote.
  • The Hub's "Analyze findings" link runs the analysis. After a sub-project switch or a failed run, the link only brought up Atlas Findings, which read No analysis yet and needed a second click. Now the link runs the analysis and opens the window on it.
  • A Design pull that removed model keys offers "Find broken references". The action runs the Unknown Flowable model key inspection over the Flowable project, so Java that still uses a removed key shows in the Inspection Results window. It also analyzes the project again in Atlas Findings, where Missing model refs lists every removed key that a model still uses, including models inside archives. Each row names the first model that uses the key and how many more do.
  • Generate Atlas Explorer on another Flowable project's folder generates that project. In a monorepo, the Project-view entry ignored the folder that was right-clicked. On a folder of another detected project it now reads Generate Atlas Explorer for apps/billing… and makes that project the active one first, so its settings apply.
  • The model-constants class stays with the Flowable project it was generated in. In a monorepo, picking another project in the Atlas Hub used to rewrite the shared constants class with that project's keys and naming, so code compiling against it broke. The class is now kept in sync only while its own project is active, and switching back brings it up to date. In a repository with several Flowable projects, the Model Constants settings page names the one it follows.
  • Generate Model Constants works while the model index is still being built. Right after opening a project or saving a model, the action ended in a "NullPointerException" balloon and wrote nothing. It now waits for the index behind its progress dialog, which you can cancel.
  • Generate Model Constants leaves its sync setting as you set it. Generating the class by hand ticked Keep the generated class in sync again, and the class was then rewritten on every model change.
  • Generate → Liquibase builds a data object's table from its service's columns. When a data object had no bundled changelog, its changelog was built from its field names, none of which are columns its service reads, and it had no primary key. It is now built the way Flowable Design builds it: the service's column names, the lookup id as the primary key and a join table per relation. Field names are used only as a labelled guess when there is no database service. A table your own Liquibase changelogs already create is shown as Already created by that file, cannot be ticked and is not written again.
  • Generate → Liquibase no longer freezes typing while it prepares its preview. On a cold index it scanned every model, walked the project and decompressed every app export in one read action, holding the editor's read lock the whole time. The model scan and the decompression now run without it, and the walk takes it only in a short read action of its own.
  • Generated data-object DTOs handle JSON fields and awkwardly named fields. A JSON field was read as a String and threw a ClassCastException for every instance that set it. It is now a Jackson JsonNode, the type the platform keeps it as. A field named after a Java keyword, such as default or case, or named bean, produced a class that did not compile. A keyword field now gets an escaped identifier and keeps its getter getDefault().
  • The Atlas Hub no longer stays on "scanning…" after a sub-project switch during a scan. Switching sub-project or saving a model while the index was being built threw that build away without starting the next one, so the Hub, the editor's markers and the model-constants class waited for some unrelated event. The new build now starts at once, and a failure of the discarded build no longer blocks it.
  • A model index that could not be built no longer rebuilds in a loop while the Atlas Playground is open. The playground retried the failed build on every index event: a full rescan every few hundred milliseconds, each one an IDE error report. It now waits for a model change or Rebuild Model Index.
  • Find Usages into models no longer blocks typing, and Cancel stops it. The search held the editor's read lock while it read every model file and archive entry. It now reads them without it, takes the lock only for a file with a hit, and stops at the next file when you cancel.
  • The editor reads your custom functions from the same place as the explorer. With a sub-project active, the editor resolved the Customization source against the repository root, missed it and read every app's functions instead. Changing the custom-function settings or switching sub-project also only took effect once a frontend file changed or the IDE restarted. The editor now resolves the source the way generation does and reads the functions again as soon as either changes.
  • Helm templates, systemd units and Java policy files are no longer opened as JSON. Atlas mapped .tpl, .service, .policy, .data and other model extensions to JSON in every project of the IDE. Those extensions are now JSON only when the file holds a JSON object, whether in a folder or inside an archive.
  • Without the embedded browser, the explorer opens in your browser, not as source. In an IDE without JCEF, the Open action, the auto-open after Generate, the balloon, the Alt+Enter intention, Atlas Findings and Recent Models opened the generated page's megabytes of HTML in the text editor and dropped the page you asked for. They now open it in your browser, on the page you asked for where your system's launcher passes the route on, or say that neither is possible here.
  • Open in Atlas Explorer on a model Atlas does not read says why. On a model in another Flowable project than the active one, in a build folder, or with no readable key, the Project-view entry used to do nothing at all. A balloon now names the reason.
  • Regenerate and the stale line work when no explorer page is selected. A project that generates only CLAUDE.md, the graph or the Playwright guide got "No Atlas Explorer yet" from Regenerate, no Regenerate after a Design pull, and no warning that those files were stale. An old page left from the default selection also kept a stale line that Regenerate could never clear. Regenerate, the pull balloon and the Hub now go by the selected artifacts, and the line reads changed since the Atlas artifacts.
  • The plugin names a dot-prefixed project's files the way the CLI does. For a folder like .DEMO-solution, the plugin wrote project.*, while the CLAUDE.md and the Playwright guide it wrote alongside pointed at .DEMO-solution.*, which did not exist.
  • The plugin manager's description covers what the plugin does today. It now names Atlas Findings, Go to Model and the Search Everywhere tab, the text-and-picture model editor, archive browsing, Compare Model with Archive, the gutter icons and the DTO and Liquibase generators. It gives menu and settings paths as the IDE shows them. The settings page no longer calls the IDE-wide environments per project.
  • The ER designer proposes the relations Design keeps in join tables. A database service's object-relation or list-relation is not a column of its table. Design keeps it in a join table of two columns, the owning row's lookup id and the referenced row's, and the runtime joins through that table. The designer understood only a column relation that Design never writes. On a real project it proposed a relation only where a data object named one: between the two tables, without columns, and mostly as a strict 1:1. Every join table sat unconnected. When a changelog creates the join table, the designer now proposes two relations from it, over exactly its columns: one to the owning table and one to the table it refers to. When none does, it proposes one relation between the two tables. When the relation names no service, the table it refers to is found through the data object field of the same name, as the runtime finds it. A data object's one-to-one is now proposed as 0..n:0..1 instead of a strict 1:1: the field holds one object, but nothing in the schema makes it unique.
  • A table's panel in the ER designer names the tables the models relate it to. A proposal shows only once both of its tables are on the canvas, and nothing said which table to add. A table's panel, and its (i) in the list, now list the related tables. Through a join table, the list names the table beyond it. Each row says whether the relation is proposed, drawn or dismissed. add puts the missing tables on the canvas beside it, with the proposals between them, and add all adds every one in a single undo step.
  • A dismissed proposal can come back. Diagram → Show N dismissed proposals again brings them all back in one undoable step, and show again in a table's related list brings back one at a time. Before, once the undo history was gone, a mis-click on × was permanent.
  • A browser copy of a project diagram no longer hides a teammate's change to the file. A copy undone back to the file, or one whose export the file now holds, follows the file again. A copy edited before the file changed keeps your work and says the file has changed in the project since, with Revert to show it. Before, it invited an export that would write over the teammate's change.
  • Schema coverage no longer lists a relation mapping as a column Liquibase lacks. A relation is kept in a join table of its own, so its mapping has no column in the service's table. Every service that related to another used to show the relation's name as mapped by the service but in no changelog, in the explorer's coverage table and in the overview.
  • ER designer panels fit on a short page. The table, relation and table-editor panels were placed before they were filled. When one opened low on the page, its last button (Remove, Delete) ran off the bottom, out of reach. Panels are now placed once filled, and they scroll inside themselves when they grow.
  • Tables added without a drop land beside what is already drawn. +, Enter, a search result and a new hand-made table now put the card in the nearest free place where you are looking, clear of other cards and frames. Before, they piled up on top of each other, and the sixth landed exactly on the first.
  • + in the ER designer's table list no longer also zooms the canvas. The list also keeps its focus after + or Enter, so the arrow keys still move through it.
  • A relation dropped onto the other table's key starts as many to one. Dropped onto a table's one-column primary key, a new relation is a lookup and starts as 0..n:1. Anywhere else it still starts as 1:0..n.
  • A slice now shows what a model contains, and who uses a variable. --slice on a process, case, decision, form or page adds its Contents exactly as the overview lists them (the steps in execution order with what follows each, the plan tree, the rule rows, the fields) and its Variables, each with the elements that set and read it. The slice of a variable, an expression or a service operation names the models that use it, and a variable's slice lists under Set by and Read by the element and how. Before, these slices said "Nothing references this node".

Older releases: see CHANGELOG.md in the repository.
